cli_body: Every action is a command. Bind them to keys, script them, or stream live events over a Unix socket into SketchyBar, JankyBorders, or your own tools.
config_body: Your whole setup is one ~/.config/KiwiDesk/init.lua file — layouts, gaps, and keybindings as plain code. It runs in a sandboxed Lua 5.5 VM behind a 500 ms watchdog, so a typo can never freeze your windows.

guide_close_p: Head back and grab KiwiDesk — it takes about a minute, and your windows will thank you.
guide_close_title: Ready to give your screen some peace?
guide_faq_1_a: No. The Settings app covers everything — layouts, gaps, monitors, shortcuts, app rules — all with clicks and sliders. Lua is there for tinkerers who want to script their setup, but it's entirely optional. Most people never open a config file.
guide_faq_1_q: Do I need to know Lua or write any code?
guide_faq_2_a: No — it works alongside them. KiwiDesk arranges the windows within your workspaces; your macOS desktops and Mission Control keep working just as they do now. You can even assign a different setup to each Mission Control desktop, so it switches automatically as you move between them.
guide_faq_2_q: Does it replace Mission Control or Spaces?
guide_faq_3_a: Yes. KiwiDesk runs entirely on your Mac, in normal user space. It only moves and resizes windows — it never reads your files, and it isn't a keylogger (its shortcuts use a built-in macOS mechanism, not keyboard monitoring). It never asks you to weaken your Mac's built-in protections.
guide_faq_4_a: KiwiDesk is a small, native macOS app built to sit quietly in the background. It only does work when your windows actually change, and its animations run at each display's own natural refresh rate. Day to day, you shouldn't notice it in the background at all. If you'd rather it not animate when switching desktops, that's a one-click setting in Behavior.
guide_faq_4_q: Will it slow down my Mac or drain the battery?
guide_faq_5_a: Quit KiwiDesk from its menu-bar icon and remove the app like any other. If you installed it with Homebrew, run brew uninstall --cask kiwidesk. The moment it's off, your windows behave exactly like normal macOS windows again — free to drag, resize, and overlap. Nothing sticks, and nothing of yours was ever changed.
guide_fav_callout_p: Nothing here is permanent. Switch layouts as often as you like — there's no wrong choice, and you can always go back. KiwiDesk only ever moves and resizes windows; it never touches your files or your apps.
guide_fav_callout_title: It's okay to change your mind
guide_fav_p1: The best way to find your layout is to try a few and feel which one suits your day. Open the Settings window from KiwiDesk's menu-bar icon, go to Layout, and pick a mode for the space you're on. Your windows rearrange right away, so you can see each one live — switch, look, switch again.
guide_fav_p2: When one feels right, it's already saved for that space. You can even give different spaces different layouts: a focused stack for writing, a wide scrolling row for research, whatever fits.

guide_gs_first_p: With the permission granted, KiwiDesk gets to work. The moment you have a window open, you'll see it settle neatly into place — filling its share of the screen, edge to edge, with no overlap. Open a second and the two share the space side by side. Nothing is buried, nothing is hunted for. You keep working the way you always do; the arranging just happens.
guide_gs_p1: Installing KiwiDesk takes about a minute. Grab it from the Mac App Store for a one-click install, or use Homebrew if you like the Terminal.
guide_gs_perm_p: The first time you open KiwiDesk, macOS asks you to grant Accessibility access. This is the normal, expected prompt — and it's the only thing KiwiDesk needs from you. To tidy your screen, it has to be able to move and resize your windows, and macOS keeps that ability behind this permission. A short onboarding wizard walks you to the right spot in System Settings › Privacy & Security › Accessibility and helps you switch it on.
guide_gs_perm_sub: The one permission it asks for
guide_gs_store_note: Requires macOS 14 or later. The App Store link is a placeholder while we finish the launch — Homebrew works today.
guide_gs_trust_1: It never asks you to disable SIP (your Mac's built-in System Integrity Protection). Your Mac's protections stay exactly as they are.
guide_gs_trust_2: It never needs Input Monitoring. Its keyboard shortcuts use a built-in macOS mechanism, so it isn't — and can't be — a keylogger.
guide_gs_trust_p: KiwiDesk stays entirely in normal user space, so the things people worry about simply aren't part of how it works:
guide_isit_p: If you spend even a little of your day dragging windows around, you'll probably feel the difference. A few everyday moments, before and after:
guide_layout_bsp: Windows split the screen into tidy panes, each new one halving the space it lands in. Balanced, edge to edge.
guide_layout_floating: The plain macOS way: windows float freely, right where you drag them. KiwiDesk leaves these ones alone.
guide_layout_grid: Everything laid out in even rows and columns — see all your windows at once, each with its own equal square.
guide_layout_monocle: One window fills the screen while the others wait quietly behind it. Pure focus, no distractions.
guide_layout_scrolling: Windows sit in a row you scroll through, like columns on a long desk — the focused one always front and center.
guide_layout_stack: One big window holds your focus, with the rest lined up neatly beside it — glance over, tap to switch.
guide_layouts_p: A “layout” is just the shape your windows arrange themselves into. KiwiDesk has six. You don't have to learn them all — most people find one they like and stay there. Here's each, in plain language.
guide_lede: No manual, no setup rituals. This is the friendly tour — what KiwiDesk does, how to make it yours, and whether it's the right fit. Scroll through, or jump to any part from the list.

guide_scenario_calls_after: Notes stay visible right beside the call — and you can give your meetings their own space, so the moment a call starts, everything's already in place. You stay present instead of shuffling windows.
guide_scenario_calls_before: The call window buries your notes. You scramble to find them, then lose the call behind something else.
guide_scenario_coder_after: Your editor and terminals tile themselves side by side, and rules send each app to its home space — code on one, docs on another. Need to check something? Jump straight to that space with a shortcut — no swiping through every desktop — then right back to the code.
guide_scenario_coder_before: Editor, a terminal or two, a browser full of docs, maybe a dashboard — you rebuild the same arrangement by hand at the start of every session.
guide_scenario_coder_name: Someone who codes or works with data
guide_scenario_designer_after: Everything snaps into a balanced arrangement the moment you open it. More screen for the work, less for the fiddling.
guide_scenario_designer_before: Canvas, layers, an inspector, a reference image — a dozen floating panels you nudge into place at the start of every session.
guide_scenario_everyday_after: Every window takes its own spot the moment it opens, nothing buried. You can even send apps to their own space — mail on one, music tucked in a corner — so each one is right where you expect it, every time.
guide_scenario_everyday_before: A browser, your messages, music, and a note or two — all stacked on top of each other. You drag one aside to find another, then lose track of where the first one went.
guide_scenario_writer_after: The draft sits front and center, sources lined up beside it. And when you need a reference that lives on another space, you flick straight there and back in a keystroke — no swiping through desktops, no losing your place.
guide_scenario_writer_before: Notes, three browser tabs pulled out into windows, and the draft — all overlapping. Half your time goes to hunting for the window you just had.
guide_settings_p: Everything is point-and-click — you never need to edit a file. Open Settings from the KiwiDesk menu in your menu bar. A sidebar on the left groups things into Design (the look and feel of the profile you're working on) and System (settings that apply everywhere). Here's what each section is for.
guide_title: A calmer Mac, in a few minutes.
guide_tour_appearance_body: Tune the little visuals — like the soft highlight that shows where a window will land when you drag it.
guide_tour_apprules_body: Automatically send an app to a chosen space every time you open it, keep certain windows floating, and pick the Settings language — all point-and-click.
guide_tour_behavior_body: Adjust how things feel: how quickly windows glide, what happens on wake from sleep, and where new windows appear.
guide_tour_layout_body: Pick a layout for each space and set the gaps between windows. This is where you choose your favorite arrangement.
guide_tour_monitors_body: Have more than one display? Pin a space to a screen by dragging it onto that monitor. Handy when you dock and undock.
guide_tour_profiles_body: Save a whole setup as a profile and switch between them — one for focused work, another for a second screen at your desk.
guide_tour_shortcuts_body: See and change the keyboard shortcuts, recorded by simply pressing the keys you want. Every conflict is flagged for you.
guide_tour_spaces_body: Name the workspaces you use — “web”, “mail”, a number — and KiwiDesk keeps each one tidy on its own.

what_body: You know the mess: a dozen windows overlapping, half of them hidden, and you spend your day nudging them around. KiwiDesk does that nudging for you. Open a window and it slots neatly into place beside the others — tidy, edge to edge, no gaps you didn’t ask for.
